newsitem.title: japan: Japan scrambles to protect nuclear plants from oil.
newsitem.headline: Japan scrambles to protect nuclear plants from oil.

text.p: Japanese officials on Saturday worked frantically to protect the world's largest group of nuclear reactors as the oil from a ruptured Russian tanker spread along a once-pristine coast.
The 15 plants dot Wakasa Bay on the Sea of Japan. The sea water is vital to keeping the reactors from overheating.

"The power plants have set up their own oil fences across the bay and we are mounting an oil collection and dispersion operation with detergent chemicals, 28 ships and six aircraft," said a spokesman for the Maritime Safety Agency.
Slicks have already come within three km (two miles) of Wakasa bay beach. They could hit the coast on Sunday, the spokesman said.
The cleanup operation, the biggest ever in Japan, is spread across a 450 km (285-mile) stretch of Japan's western coast.
Officials on Saturday said spotter planes found new slicks heading farther northeast that would probably hit previously unaffected parts of the coast.

Maritime safety officials said their earlier estimate of 3,700 tonnes (26,000 barrels) of oil spilled from the 13,157-tonne tanker Nakhodka was far too low. The 26-year-old tanker was carrying 19,000 tonnes (133,000 barrels) of fuel oil when it broke up in stormy seas on January 2.
The incoming sludge, which has taken on the consistency of thick mud as it floats in the water, is posing an unaccustomed threat to the nuclear plants.
"We've done disaster exercises for meltdowns and so on but we've never done one for an oil slick threat," said Kenzo Furuichi, deputy manager of the Japan Atomic Power Co's Tsuruga power plant.
The gradual sinking of the oil as it gets thicker can clog water intake pipes, set about five metres (16 feet) below sea level.
"We don't believe that is at all likely, although nature cannot be at all predicted," said one official, who asked not to be identified.
Kansai Electric Power Co, which operates 11 reactors around Wakasa Bay, was operating as usual on Saturday and officials said they had no plans yet to lower power production.
The utility serves Osaka, Japan's second-biggest metropolitan area. The plants generate 27 percent of the company's total power output.
Special craft, government workers, fishermen and volunteers meanwhile continued their attempt to collect the heavy oil, often one bucket at a time.
Isao Yamada, head of Maizuru Fishermen's Union, was among those out on boats scooping oil out of the sea in a bid to protect his way of life.
"Many of the union's 437 members are getting on in years and their legs and backs are too weak to do this work in heavy seas," he said.
"Volunteers would be welcome, but I'm afraid most would get seasick out there."
Russia's Civil Defence and Emergencies Ministry is meanwhile sending two ships designed to gather the oil from seawater.
The Russian owners of the tanker said they would pay for the mess.
The Interfax news agency quoted Sergei Vitkazov, chief executive of Prisco Traffic Ltd, which owns the vessel, as saying that the company would use insurance money to pay for compensation.
